khazars.name: Khazars
khazars.summary: A semi-nomadic Turkic people who built a major trading empire from about 650 to 965 CE spanning southern Russia, Ukraine, and Kazakhstan, with a ruling elite that converted to Judaism in the 8th century.

kievan-rus.name: Kievan Rus'
kievan-rus.summary: The first East Slavic state, later a group of principalities, spanning the late 9th to mid-13th century from the White Sea to the Black Sea under the Rurik dynasty.

volga-bulgaria.name: Volga Bulgaria
volga-bulgaria.summary: A multi-ethnic Bulgar state that existed from the 9th to 13th centuries near the meeting of the Volga and Kama rivers, controlling trade among Norse, Cuman, and other peoples.

chersonesus.name: Chersonesus
chersonesus.summary: An ancient Greek colony founded around the 6th century BC on Crimea's coast, later known in medieval Greek as Cherson; it operated for a time as a democracy and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

volga-trade-route.name: Volga trade route
volga-trade-route.summary: A medieval trade route linking Northern Europe with the Caspian Sea and Persia via the Volga River, used by Rus' merchants to trade with Muslim lands as far as Baghdad.

kasha.name: Kasha
kasha.summary: A porridge usually made from buckwheat, called kasha in Slavic languages, where it can also mean any cooked grain and was long a Russian household staple.

rod-slavic-religion.name: Rod
rod-slavic-religion.summary: Personification of family, ancestors and fate in pre-Christian East and South Slavic belief, honoured alongside fairy-like Rozhanitsy who were said to influence events such as childbirth.

deities-and-fairies-of-fate-in-slavic-my.name: Rozhanitsy
deities-and-fairies-of-fate-in-slavic-my.summary: Invisible spirits or deities of fate in pre-Christian Slavic belief, linked to pregnancy, motherhood, marriage and female ancestors, usually described as a group of three.
deities-and-fairies-of-fate-in-slavic-my.source_title: Deities and fairies of fate in Slavic mythology

isinglass.name: Isinglass
isinglass.summary: A form of collagen made from dried fish swim bladders, traditionally from sturgeon, used to clarify beer and wine and for specialised gluing.

vladimir-the-great.name: Vladimir the Great
vladimir-the-great.summary: Prince of Novgorod from 970 and Grand Prince of Kiev from 978 until 1015, who converted to Christianity in 988 and Christianized Kievan Rus'; canonised as a saint by both the Catholic and Orthodox churches.

hagia-sophia.name: Hagia Sophia
hagia-sophia.summary: A monumental building in Istanbul completed in 537 CE, serving in turn as a Byzantine cathedral, a mosque, a museum, and again a mosque since 2020.

cross-in-square.name: Cross-in-square plan
cross-in-square.summary: A church floor plan with a square centre containing an internal cross shape topped by a dome, the dominant style of church architecture in the middle and late Byzantine Empire.

rus-people.name: Rus'
rus-people.summary: An early medieval people, generally held to be Norsemen mainly from Sweden, who settled and ruled trade routes between the Baltic and Black Sea from the 8th to 11th centuries and gave their name to Russia.

michael-iii.name: Michael III
michael-iii.summary: Byzantine emperor from 842 to 867, last of the Amorian dynasty, whose reign—despite his later reputation as a drunkard—saw a resurgence of Byzantine power before his assassination.

bulgars.name: Bulgars
bulgars.summary: Turkic semi-nomadic warrior tribes active in the Pontic–Caspian steppe and Volga region from the 5th to 7th centuries, who later founded the First Bulgarian Empire in 681 and became ancestors of modern Bulgarians.

krum.name: Krum
krum.summary: Khan of the First Bulgarian Empire (c. 796/803–814) whose reign doubled Bulgaria's territory and produced its first known written law code.

omurtag-of-bulgaria.name: Omurtag
omurtag-of-bulgaria.summary: Khan of Bulgaria from 814 to 831, known as 'the Builder,' who signed a lasting peace treaty with the Byzantine Empire and oversaw major architectural projects.

primary-chronicle.name: Primary Chronicle
primary-chronicle.summary: A chronicle of Kievan Rus' history from about 850 to 1110, compiled around the 1110s and considered a fundamental source for the earliest history of the East Slavs.

oleg-the-wise.name: Oleg the Wise
oleg-the-wise.summary: Varangian prince of the Rus' who succeeded Rurik as ruler of Novgorod, conquered Kiev and became its prince, and laid the foundations of Kievan Rus'; he died in 912.

thrace.name: Thrace
thrace.summary: A historical and geographical region in Southeast Europe, roughly matching the Roman province of Thrace, spanning parts of modern Bulgaria, Greece and Turkey.

sviatoslav-i.name: Sviatoslav I
sviatoslav-i.summary: Prince of Kiev from 945 to 972 whose campaigns helped destroy the powers of Khazaria and the First Bulgarian Empire, carving out the largest state in Europe at the time; he remained a lifelong pagan.

first-bulgarian-empire.name: First Bulgarian Empire
first-bulgarian-empire.summary: Medieval Bulgarian state founded in 680–681 by Bulgars under Asparuh, which by the 9th and 10th centuries rivaled the Byzantine Empire and adopted Christianity in 864.

pechenegs.name: Pechenegs
pechenegs.summary: A semi-nomadic Turkic people from Central Asia who controlled the steppes of southeast Europe and Crimea in the 9th and 10th centuries, waging over two centuries of wars against Rus'.

varangian-guard.name: Varangian Guard
varangian-guard.summary: An elite bodyguard unit of the Byzantine emperors, mainly composed of Norse and later Anglo-Saxon warriors, formally established under Emperor Basil II in 988.

basil-ii.name: Basil II
basil-ii.summary: Byzantine emperor from 976 to 1025, nicknamed the Bulgar Slayer for conquering the First Bulgarian Empire; his 49-year reign was the longest of any Roman emperor.

sarkel.name: Sarkel
sarkel.summary: A limestone-and-brick fortress built by the Khazars with Byzantine help in the 830s or 840s on the Don River, its name meaning 'white house.'

photios-i-of-constantinople.name: Photios I of Constantinople
photios-i-of-constantinople.summary: Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from 858 to 867 and 877 to 886 (c. 815–893), regarded as the most important intellectual of his era and a central figure in the conversion of the Slavs to Christianity.

vyatichi.name: Vyatichi
vyatichi.summary: A tribe of early East Slavs living around the Oka, Moskva, and Don rivers, known for a self-governing society without princes and for later paying tribute to the Khazars and Kievan princes.

oghuz-turks.name: Oghuz Turks
oghuz-turks.summary: A western Turkic people whose 8th-century tribal confederation in Central Asia became the ancestors of today's Turkmen, Azerbaijanis and Turks.

orestias.name: Orestias / Adrianople
orestias.summary: An ancient Greek settlement in Thrace, later refounded by Hadrian as Adrianople, near present-day Edirne, Turkey.

bardas-skleros.name: Bardas Skleros
bardas-skleros.summary: Byzantine general who led a wide-scale rebellion in Asia Minor against Emperor Basil II between 976 and 979.

battle-of-arcadiopolis-970.name: Battle of Arcadiopolis
battle-of-arcadiopolis-970.summary: A 970 battle in which a Byzantine army under Bardas Skleros ambushed and defeated an invading Rus' force allied with Bulgarians, Pechenegs and Magyars, buying time for Emperor John I Tzimiskes to later defeat Sviatoslav.

varangians.name: Varangians
varangians.summary: Viking traders, warriors and settlers, mostly from Sweden, who founded the state of Kievan Rus' and other principalities from the 8th-9th centuries.

veliky-novgorod.name: Veliky Novgorod
veliky-novgorod.summary: One of Russia's oldest cities, first mentioned in the 9th century; center of the Novgorod Republic from 1136 to 1478 and a major trading link to northwestern Europe via the Hanseatic League.

rurik.name: Rurik
rurik.summary: Varangian chieftain of the Rus' (died 879), traditionally invited to rule Novgorod in 862, and regarded as founder of the Rurik dynasty and of the Russian monarchy.

constantine-vi.name: Constantine VI
constantine-vi.summary: Byzantine emperor from 780 to 797, crowned co-emperor at age five, who was later deposed and blinded by his own mother, Empress Irene, who then ruled alone.

struma-river.name: Struma valley
struma-river.summary: The valley of the Struma river, which flows through Bulgaria and Greece and was anciently known as the Strymon.

kardam-of-bulgaria.name: Kardam
kardam-of-bulgaria.summary: Ruler of the First Bulgarian Empire from 777 until sometime between 796 and 803.

emirate-of-crete.name: Emirate of Crete
emirate-of-crete.summary: An Arab Islamic state on Crete from the late 820s to 961, used as a base for Muslim raiding fleets against Byzantine territory until the Byzantines retook the island.

siege-of-dorostolon.name: Dorostolon
siege-of-dorostolon.summary: An ancient city (modern Silistra) that was besieged in 971, when Byzantine forces under John I Tzimiskes defeated an army of Kievan Rus'.

old-church-slavonic.name: Old Church Slavonic
old-church-slavonic.summary: The first Slavic literary language, standardized by 9th-century missionaries Cyril and Methodius for translating scripture, and ancestor of the liturgical Church Slavonic still used today.

bylina.name: Bylina
bylina.summary: A traditional Russian oral epic poem loosely based on history but embellished with fantasy, originating in the era of Kievan Rus'.

old-east-slavic.name: Old East Slavic
old-east-slavic.summary: A language used by the East Slavs from the 7th–8th to 13th–14th centuries that later split into the Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian/Ruthenian languages.

preslav-literary-school.name: Preslav Literary School
preslav-literary-school.summary: The first literary school of the medieval First Bulgarian Empire, established by Boris I in 886 and moved to the new capital, Veliki Preslav, under Simeon I in 893.

ohrid-literary-school.name: Ohrid Literary School
ohrid-literary-school.summary: One of two major cultural centers of the First Bulgarian Empire, founded in 886 in Ohrid, where Clement taught using the Glagolitic and later Cyrillic alphabets.

glagolitic-script.name: Glagolitic script
glagolitic-script.summary: The oldest-known Slavic alphabet, created in the 9th century by the monk Cyril to translate Greek scripture into Old Church Slavonic, later largely replaced by Cyrillic.

novgorod-codex.name: Novgorod Codex
novgorod-codex.summary: The oldest known book of the Kievan Rus', a wax-tablet palimpsest found in Novgorod in 2000 and dated to around 1000 CE, reused repeatedly by its owner over two or three decades.

volkhov-river.name: Volkhov
volkhov-river.summary: A 224-kilometre river in northwestern Russia connecting Lake Ilmen to Lake Ladoga, flowing past the city of Veliky Novgorod.

dnieper.name: Dnieper
dnieper.summary: A major European river about 2,200 km long, flowing from Russia through Belarus and Ukraine to the Black Sea; the longest river of Ukraine and Belarus.

askold-and-dir.name: Askold and Dir
askold-and-dir.summary: The earliest recorded Varangian rulers of Kiev, said to have died in 882, known from the Primary Chronicle and other early Rus' sources.

boyar.name: Boyar
boyar.summary: A member of the highest-ranking feudal nobility in medieval Eastern European states such as Kievan Rus', Bulgaria, Moldavia and Wallachia, ranking just below princes and tsars.

rurikids.name: Rurikid dynasty
rurikids.summary: The dynasty founded by Rurik in 862, which ruled Kievan Rus' and its principalities and later the Tsardom of Russia for over 700 years until 1598.

knyaz.name: Knyaz
knyaz.summary: A historical Slavic noble and royal title, usually translated as prince, king or duke depending on context, derived from the Germanic word for king.

anti-normanism.name: Anti-Normanism
anti-normanism.summary: A theory holding that Kievan Rus' arose from East Slavic tribes rather than Scandinavian Varangians, opposing the mainstream 'Normanist' view of its origins.

byzantine-rite.name: Byzantine Rite
byzantine-rite.summary: A liturgical tradition of the Eastern Christian church of Constantinople, marked by long, complex services, frequent veneration of icons, and distinctive chanting.

tengrism.name: Tengrism
tengrism.summary: A belief system from the Eurasian steppes based on shamanism and animism and centered on the sky god Tengri, once the state religion of several medieval Turkic and Mongol states.

old-great-bulgaria.name: Old Great Bulgaria
old-great-bulgaria.summary: A 7th-century Turkic nomadic empire formed by the Onogur-Bulgars on the steppe north of the Black Sea, which broke apart after defeats by Avars, Slavs and Khazars.

olga-of-kiev.name: Olga of Kiev
olga-of-kiev.summary: Regent of Kievan Rus' for her son Sviatoslav from 945 to 957, later baptized as the first Rurikid ruler to convert to Christianity, and venerated as a saint.

korchak-culture.name: Korchak culture
korchak-culture.summary: Archaeological culture of 6th- and 7th-century East Slavs settled along rivers in what is now northwestern Ukraine and southern Belarus, part of the early Slavic Prague-Korchak horizon.

suzdal.name: Suzdal
suzdal.summary: A town in Vladimir Oblast, Russia, that became capital of the Rostov-Suzdal principality in the early 12th century, a forerunner of the Russian state; now part of Russia's historic Golden Ring.

murom.name: Murom
murom.summary: One of the oldest cities in Russia, first mentioned in 862 on the Oka River, once center of the Principality of Murom.

polotsk.name: Polotsk
polotsk.summary: A town on the Dvina River in Vitebsk Region, Belarus, serving as the administrative center of Polotsk District, with a population of about 79,000.

finno-ugric-languages.name: Finno-Ugric peoples
finno-ugric-languages.summary: A traditional grouping of Uralic language speakers, including Hungarian, Finnish and Estonian, a term that came into general use in the late 19th century.

kurgan.name: Kurgan
kurgan.summary: A type of burial mound built over a grave, originating on the Pontic–Caspian steppe and spreading through Central Asia and Europe, with the earliest examples dating to the fourth millennium BC.

luka-raikovetska-culture.name: Luka-Raikovetska culture
luka-raikovetska-culture.summary: An early medieval archaeological culture of the Early Slavs in Eastern Europe, lasting from the late 7th to early 10th century, that shaped later Kievan Rus' traditions.

plisnesk-archaeological-complex.name: Plisnesk
plisnesk-archaeological-complex.summary: An early medieval fortified settlement of tens of thousands of people, part of the Luka-Raikovetska culture and a centre of the Croat tribe, destroyed around 992–993.
